Ti–O solid–gas thermodynamics

Calculate oxide phase stability, vacancy distribution within a particle, and isolated-vacancy loss during pretreatment.

Vacancy distribution

R600 during H₂ reduction and CO₂ reoxidation at 600 °C. The calculation follows oxygen vacancies and Ti³⁺ from the surface to the centre of a 900 nm rutile particle.

R600 · 600 °C

Particle diameter900 nm
Outer 30 nm barrier1.6 eV
Interior barrier2.2 eV

The transport barriers are assumed. Measured gas-release rates set the surface source and sink. The initial particle has no defects.

Tested transport cases

Each row uses the same R600 source and sink. “Completed” means that the calculation reached 600 s of reoxidation. A stopped calculation records its last computed time.

Method

Particle geometry and site counts

The calculation uses a spherical rutile particle with radius R = 450 nm at T = 873.15 K. Depth z is measured from the surface. Four explicit (110) trilayers describe the outer 1.30 nm; 320 spherical cells describe the interior. The (110) area fraction is 0.75. Site capacities count each oxygen and titanium site once.

z=R−r,NOtot=2NAM,NTitot=NAM
Asp=3ρR,A110=2alatclat,CBRI(z)=0.75AspA110(1−zR)2

These equations give sites per gram when lengths use consistent units. M = 79.866 g mol⁻¹, ρ = 4.2487 g cm⁻³, alat = 0.4594 nm and clat = 0.2958 nm. Each trilayer has one bridging oxygen, two in-plane oxygens, one sub-bridging oxygen and two titanium sites per surface cell. Interior capacities are assigned by shell volume after subtraction of the explicit sites.

fshell=(1−zloR)3−(1−zhiR)3

Local states and their energies

A joint cell contains one bridging oxygen site and two Ti sites in the second trilayer. State a has v vacancies, n excess electrons, energy E and multiplicity g. An excess electron represents a Ti³⁺ polaron. The vacancy and electrons occupy different planes, so they receive different electrostatic potentials.

The displayed case uses Δ = −1.2 eV, B = 0.8 eV and εe = 0. The last three rows represent three neutral vacancy–polaron arrangements. The gaps use the PBE state set in the archived code. The multiplicity 2 counts equivalent electron positions. This eight-state construction, Δ and B are model assumptions.

Cjoint=min(CBRI,CTi,22)

Unused bridging sites have binary occupancy with energy Δ + B. Other oxygen sites and free Ti sites have binary occupancy with zero reference energy. The interior uses ideal binary states for vacancies and electrons.

State probabilities and chemical potentials

The vacancy chemical potential μV,i varies between transport cells. The electron chemical potential μe is common to the particle. At each time step, electrons and local state populations relax at the current vacancy distribution.

hda=Eda+2vdaeϕV,d−ndaeϕe,d−vdaμV,i(d)−ndaμe
wda=gdaexp(−hdakBT),Zd=∑awda,pda=wdaZd,xda=Cdpda

x is the state population and C is the number of cells. φV,d is the potential at the oxygen plane; φe,d is the potential at the Ti plane. For a single binary site, the same expression gives the occupancy relation below.

lnθV1−θV=−EV+2eϕ−μVkBT,lnθe1−θe=−Ee−eϕ−μekBT
NV=∑d,avdaxda,Ne=∑d,andaxda=2NV

Free energy and electrostatic potential

The free energy contains local state energies, configurational entropy and electrostatic energy. In these equations, N and x are particle counts per gram and q is charge per gram. The implementation converts these quantities to µmol g⁻¹ and uses eV for energies.

F=∑d,axdaEda+kBT∑d,axdalnxdaCdgda+12∑iqiϕi,qi=e(2NV,i−Ne,i)

Each vacancy contributes +2e and each electron contributes −e. Spherical Poisson electrostatics gives the potential. The relative permittivity is 64.

−1r2∂∂r(r2ϵ0ϵr∂ϕ∂r)=e(2cV−ce),ϵr=64

c denotes number density. The shell calculation sums the potentials of charged spherical shells. This also fixes the zero of potential at infinity. The total particle charge is zero.

ϕi=14πϵ0ϵr∑jQjmax(ri,rj),∑jQj=0

Q is the charge of a shell in one particle. The solver uses the equivalent tridiagonal inverse of this shell-potential matrix. State probabilities and potential are solved together.

Depth-dependent vacancy mobility

The outer 30 nm uses an effective migration barrier of 1.6 eV. The interior uses 2.2 eV. The same mobility applies during reduction and reoxidation. These barriers define the displayed tested case.

Em(z)={1.6eV,0≤z<30nm2.2eV,z≥30nm
D(z)=ah2ν06exp[−Em(z)kBT],ah=0.3nm,ν0=1013s−1

A face that crosses 30 nm uses the diffusion resistance of both parts of the interval. ℓo is the length within the outer region.

Di+1/2=Δziℓo/Do+(Δzi−ℓo)/Db

Vacancy flux between cells

Cells are numbered from surface to centre. Ji is the vacancy amount per unit time moving inward from cell i to cell i + 1. The finite-volume flux includes occupied and empty sites on both sides of the face.

θi=NV,iCO,i,αi=μV,ikBT,ηi=αi−lnθi1−θi,δi=ηi+1−ηi
b(δ)=δexp(δ)−1,b(0)=1
Ji=Gi[b(δi)θi(1−θi+1)−b(−δi)θi+1(1−θi)]
Gi=Di+1/2ρO4πri+1/22Δzi

ρO is the oxygen-site inventory per particle volume. The first twelve face conductances also receive the (110) area factor 0.75. With this sign convention, diffusion follows decreasing vacancy chemical potential.

D=kBT∑iJi(αi−αi+1)≥0

Initial condition and measured surface exchange

Reduction starts with zero vacancies and zero excess electrons. The measured oxygen-removal rate sets the surface input. Reoxidation starts from the final reduction state. The measured CO-formation rate sets oxygen incorporation: one CO molecule fills one vacancy and removes two excess electrons.

NV(0)=Ne(0)=0,NVred(t)=∫0tsred(τ)dτ,Ne(t)=2NV(t)
NVox(t)=NVred(1800s)−QCO(t),Jsurfaceox=−dQCOdt

The reduction rate is piecewise linear; its integral uses the trapezoidal rule. For reoxidation, the code integrates the measured rates at the input times and applies a running maximum to the cumulative curve. Linear interpolation of that cumulative curve supplies a non-negative oxygen-incorporation rate between input times. Endpoint rates are extended to the stage boundaries. The curves retain their measured scale.

Qkraw=∑j<ksj+sj+12(tj+1−tj),Qk=maxm≤kQmraw

The centre has zero vacancy flux. Reduction lasts 1800 s and reoxidation lasts 600 s. The calculation predicts the internal distribution under these measured boundary amounts.

Time steps and coupled numerical solution

Backward Euler updates each cell inventory. J−1 denotes surface input; JL−1 = 0 denotes centre flux.

NV,ik+1−NV,ik=Δt(Ji−1k+1−Jik+1)

The unknown vector contains one vacancy chemical potential per cell, one electron chemical potential and one potential per electrostatic shell. Newton iteration solves local vacancy balance, total electron balance and Poisson electrostatics together.

y=(α0,…,αL−1,μe/kBT,eϕ0/kBT,…),H(y)Δy=−R(y)
ynew=y+λΔy,0<λ≤1

R is the coupled residual vector and H is its analytic Jacobian. Row scaling and a line search control the Newton step. A failed time step is retried at half its duration. The maximum step is 2.5 s during reduction and 0.05 s during reoxidation. Near-empty cells use the archived least-norm treatment of the null tail. The validation checks test local inventory balance, total vacancy and electron counts, Poisson consistency and non-negative transport dissipation. Figures show saved time checkpoints.

Validation

The integrated reduction source gives 95.719 µmol O g⁻¹. The measured R600 inventory is 94 µmol O g⁻¹. The endpoint difference is 1.83%. After 600 s of reoxidation, 14.194 µmol O g⁻¹ of vacancies remain and 81.525 µmol O g⁻¹ of vacancies have been filled. Both histories use the same depth-dependent mobility.

The source snapshot, input rates, raw results, and checks are stored in pilot/joint_state_release. The previous equilibrium distribution calculations remain in the source history and data archive.

Method

Scope. C–H–O–N / Ti–O Gibbs equilibrium. Gas registry in this version: CO2, H2, CO, H2O, N2, O2. Hydrocarbon species (CH4), graphite, nitrides, and the rutile TiO2−x solution phase are not included in this version. The calculation is a closed, finite-inventory equilibrium between one gas charge and one solid charge, not a flow-reactor steady state. Every reported value is gibbs_min.

Gas-phase RWGS atlas

The atlas first removes the solid from the question. For a fresh H2/CO2 feed it solves the single equilibrium

CO2+H2⇌CO+H2O

on a one-mole fresh-gas basis. Because the reaction has no net change in gas moles, this ideal-gas conversion ceiling is independent of total pressure. The separate gas–solid curve then uses the oxide mass, gas charge, pressure, and volume from the input panel. A difference between the two curves means oxygen exchange with the solid has entered the equilibrium result.

Finite gas–solid contact

The solver computes the minimum of the total Gibbs energy

G=∑i∈gasniμi+∑j∈solidmjμj∘(T)μi=μi∘(T)+RTln(yiPP∘)

subject to the elemental balance 𝐀𝐳=𝐛 and 𝐳≥0, where 𝐳 collects all gas and solid amounts. Gases form an ideal mixture; each condensed phase is a pure line compound at unit activity. The inputs defining b are the initial gas composition, the gas charge ng,0=PV/(RTcharge), and the initial solid phase and mass. The equilibrium phase split is an output.

min𝐳≥0G(𝐳;T,P),𝐀𝐳=𝐛yi=ni∑k∈gasnkbe=∑i∈gasaieni+∑j∈solidajemj

Amounts are in mol; standard chemical potentials are per mole of the species or solid formula unit. aie is the number of atoms of element e in species i. The gas constant and chemical potentials must use the same energy unit, and P/P∘ is dimensionless.

Active set. Condensed phases are enumerated as candidates: every single phase and every phase pair (the phase rule allows two line compounds in an M–O system at fixed T and P; N2 adds no solid component). For each candidate the equilibrium conditions are

μi=∑eaieλe(i∈gas)μj∘=tjλTi+ojλO(j∈active solids)

solved by Newton iteration in the element potentials λ with the gas in logarithmic coordinates. Condensed amounts follow linearly from the Ti and O balances through the combination O − ρhost·Ti, which removes the host oxygen symbolically; coexisting phases are resolved down to ~10−41 mol. A phase outside the candidate is not a variable and is exactly zero in the result.

Stability criterion. Each inactive phase carries a reduced cost rj = μ°j − tjλTi − ojλO, reported per formula unit and per mole of oxygen (defj = 2tj − oj; defj = 1 for each TiO2→Magnéli step). The problem is convex, so a feasible candidate with all rj ≥ 0 is the global minimum. Candidates are not ranked by total Gibbs energy, whose differences can fall below double-precision resolution. Reduced costs at zero within tolerance are reported as phase coexistence.

Phase stability and iteration

Element potentials enforce atom conservation. Differentiating the constrained Gibbs energy gives the gas equilibrium conditions above and the solid-phase reduced costs:

ℒ=G−λT(𝐀𝐳−𝐛)rj=μj∘−tjλTi−ojλOmj≥0,rj≥0,mjrj=0

A phase present at equilibrium has zero reduced cost. A positive reduced cost means that adding an infinitesimal amount of that phase raises the constrained Gibbs energy. For reduced titanium oxides, the plotted oxygen-normalized value is

Δj=2tj−oj,rj,O=rjΔj(Δj>0)

Each candidate phase set is solved iteratively. With the balance and equilibrium equations collected in 𝐅, the Newton correction satisfies

𝐉(𝐮k)Δ𝐮k=−𝐅(𝐮k)𝐮k+1=𝐮k+αkΔ𝐮k,0<αk≤1

Here 𝐉 is the Jacobian, 𝐮 contains the solver coordinates, and αk controls the step length. The iteration stops when the equilibrium equations and atom balances meet the numerical tolerance; the remaining phases are then checked for stability.

Oxygen-free feeds. Under pure H2 or N2 the single-phase candidate leaves the gas with zero oxygen inventory, and the derivative of G toward forming a trace of O-bearing gas together with a reduced phase diverges. The solver therefore reports the two-phase buffer with a finite trace amount; under sealed N2 this trace is the equilibrium result. An O2 impurity at the ppm level is sufficient to suppress reduction, with a positive margin.

The oxygen-potential margin used by earlier versions of this site equals the reduced cost per mole of oxygen (the dual of the same minimisation); it is reported in the phase-stability checks below. Independent verification is provided by an 80-digit reference implementation and by the NIST–Waldner data comparison in the validation section below.

SampleTreatmentnV,tot rCOrCO fitted nisonassoc nbelow

Inventories in µmol-O g⁻¹; rates in µmol g⁻¹ s⁻¹.

Method

The titration gives the total oxygen removed per sample. The model splits it into three populations,

nV,tot=niso+nassoc+nbelow

Removal is generated uniformly over the reduction time, g=nV,tot/tred. A new vacancy joins the surface active region of capacity ns with probability ffree=1−(niso+nassoc)/ns and otherwise goes below it. Two isolated vacancies associate at second order.

g=nV,tottred,q=niso+nassocffree=1−qns

Population balances

dnisodt=gffree−2klossnsniso2dnassocdt=2klossnsniso2dnbelowdt=g(1−ffree)

All three populations start at zero. Associated vacancies are counted as vacancies, rather than as pairs, so association transfers equal amounts between the first two populations. Summing the balances gives

ddt(niso+nassoc+nbelow)=gniso(t)+nassoc(t)+nbelow(t)=gt

Reduction to one equation. With q=niso+nassoc the loss term cancels from the sum:

dqdt=g(1−qns)q(t)=ns[1−exp(−gtns)]nbelow(t)=gt−q(t)

Thus ffree=exp(−gt/ns), and a single scalar equation remains:

dnisodt=gexp(−gtns)−2klossnsniso2niso(0)=0kloss=νeffexp(−ElosskBT)nassoc=q−niso

At t=tred, the sum of the three populations equals the measured total inventory. Populations and capacity use µmol O g⁻¹, time uses s, g uses µmol O g⁻¹ s⁻¹, and kloss and νeff use s⁻¹. Eloss and kBT use eV. The scalar equation goes to an implicit integrator (Radau in the package, Strang splitting in the browser), which stays stable wherever a parameter search tries a small Eloss with a large νeff.

Rate. The initial CO formation rate is taken proportional to niso with one coefficient for every sample; rates are compared as ratios normalised to R600.

rCO(sample)rCO(R600)=niso(sample)niso(R600)

Fit. Three parameters, ns (bounded between the bridging row and the bridging row plus the first subsurface oxygen layer, 13.6 to 67.8 µmol-O g⁻¹), Eloss and log10 νeff, against five rates. The rates span 86-fold, so the residual definition moves the fit: a log or relative residual recovers the reported parameters, a raw residual is dominated by one sample.

Inputs and limits. niso is inferred from the measured rates. The rates constrain niso; nassoc and nbelow follow from the assumed second-order loss law, uniform generation and constant capacity ns. Surface area is held constant through the 1000 °C treatment (sample BET values unavailable). The model contains no reconstruction, cluster geometry or shear structure. Eloss and log νeff are effective parameters of the net isolated-vacancy loss rate constant kloss.

Validation

Numerical fit

Browser against package

The browser integrates the same scalar equation as the Python package with a different integrator, Strang splitting against Radau, and a parity gate holds the two to a relative 1e−6 across the reduction series and the parameter search. The reported parameters reproduce the supplement's table at the reported digits.
